holidays.name: National Peanut Brittle Day
holidays.description: A day for snapping, crunching, and trying not to lose a filling. Celebrate by eating the glassy, golden candy of caramelized sugar and roasted peanuts. You can also make a batch at home and pretend you're a candy scientist.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial food observance. It started as a nod to one of America's oldest homemade confections.
holidays.funFact: Brittle is traditionally cooked to the 'hard crack' stage, around 300°F. That's hot enough that candy makers treat it with serious respect.

holidays.name: National Green Juice Day
holidays.description: A day to raise a tall glass of liquid lawn clippings, otherwise known as kale, spinach, cucumber, celery, and friends. It's a chance to give your body a vitamin boost and see whether you can drink a salad with a straight face.
holidays.origin: This is an unofficial wellness and food observance. It grew out of the popularity of juicing and the start-of-year healthy-eating push.
holidays.funFact: Many green juices add a little apple or lemon, because that's often what makes the drink taste better.

holidays.name: National Spouses Day
holidays.description: A day to appreciate your husband, wife, or partner. Think small gestures, a heartfelt note, or finally doing the dishes without being asked. It's the day after a certain 'opposite' day, so no reverse psychology allowed.
holidays.origin: It was created in the early 2000s by Patricia Larson of Ohio as a way to recognize the people we marry and live with.
holidays.funFact: It comes right after the start-of-year rush, so it often gets an extra bit of attention as people look for ways to build good habits as a couple.
